title: Learning piano: mother, Mrs. Asett and ragtime on player pianos
summary: His mother encouraged him, he took lessons from Mrs. Asett, and he kept straying to ragtime tunes heard on player pianos and phonographs.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Okay. How about a little bit on where you learned how to play piano and what extent of formal training you had, and maybe how you first got interested in jazz piano?

Well, I guess, Charlie, I had a desire to play music ever from the time that I could remember myself, although I don't say that I was a child prodigy because I don't remember playing when I was two years old or a year and a half old. But when I was about six or seven, I think I played drums when I was at school, a little school band. And then later on, my mother, who played piano, a little bit, who did not read very much, but she knew enough to be able to encourage me. And it used to fascinate me just to sit down and watch her play and listen to her play little pieces. So she gave me a lot of encouragement. And, in fact, she told me that she wanted me to start taking some private lessons after she had already given me some ideas about the scale and the notes and so forth, which I had quite an advantage when I began taking.
Did you study privately for any great length of time, or did you more or less go off on your own with listening to pianists about town or what?

Well, I started with this lady by the name of Mrs. Essett. How do you spell that? A-S-E-T-T. And she was a very wonderful person who had the patience of a saint because I did not want to study the sort of things that she was giving me. And she insisted that I should learn more of the rudiments of the basic things, you know, that you had to know. But it seemed like everywhere I'd come out I'd listen to the old player piano rolls and the old Edison phonographs in those days, you know, playing the old Dixieland records and listening to the old jazz bands march up and down the street and all that sort of thing. And, well, everywhere I turned around I mean I just heard jazz music. And of course in those days it was more commonly referred to as ragtime, you know. Right. Right. A lot of the people didn't say, well do you play jazz? Because I know that when I was going to my teacher I told her, I said, oh, I said, you know, I love to play some of those ragtime tunes that I hear on the player piano. And she says, well, she said, that'll come in time, you know. I said, yeah, but that's just it. I says, I don't want to wait. I says, I'd like to play now. So she had a hard time keeping me from digging into some of these ragtime tunes that were out at the time, like Maple Leaf Rag and some of the other tunes, Spaghetti Rag, and well, you know, just a couple, name a few.
